title: The Supremacy of Jesus' Name
english: That no name greater than Jesus has been named among those on earth, the Gospel testifies, where 'the angel' said to Mary, 'do not fear,' for 'you have found favor with God. And behold, you will conceive in your womb and give birth to a son, and you shall call his name Jesus. This one will be great, and will be called the Son of the Most High' (Luke 1:30-32).

It is also clear from the prophecy of Zechariah, having prophesied long ago concerning this name, for he says, 'the Lord showed to me Jesus the great priest, standing before the face of an angel of the Lord, and the devil was standing at his right hand to oppose him. And the Lord said to the devil: the Lord who has chosen Jerusalem rebuke you' (Zechariah 3:1). For when did he rebuke him? When he joined to himself by word the man loved by him. 'The one who has chosen,' he says, 'Jerusalem,' making it clear that this is our [Jerusalem], concerning which the apostle says, 'but our Jerusalem is above; for this one serves with her children' (Galatians 4:26).

For just then in that same great Jerusalem, that is, in our church, having come, he rebuked the devil according to the prophecy, saying, 'Go behind me, Satan, for you are a stumbling block to me' (Matthew 16:23). This, therefore, is the great priest, whose type Jesus was saving.

For it was not possible for that one to be called a great priest, even though he had become glorious among all, without Moses being named great (for Moses was not yet great, since he was heard to be a servant of God and was named god of Pharaoh by him, that god). And if anyone thinks to say Jesus is great according to this, that he was worthy to lead the people into the holy land and did many other wonderful things, let him know also through this, that the greatness spoken of Jesus did not differ so much in the actual matter from the typical, but rather in the small matter of being about to lead his own people into this great Jerusalem later on.

Not only, therefore, does the apostle say that he is the firstborn of the 'new creation,' but also firstborn 'from the dead,' through no other means, it seems to me, but so that through the firstborn 'of the dead,' just as it is said, 'firstborn of all creation,' he might be able to be known. For our Lord Jesus Christ did not rise first from the dead; rather, he who rose through the prophet Elisha rose earlier, and Lazarus rose before his own resurrection, and in the time of the passion 'many bodies of those asleep' rose.

Now let us examine one explicit thing written by Asterius; for he said: 'For another is the Father, who begat from himself the only-begotten Word and firstborn of all creation.' Having joined both [terms] as only-begotten and firstborn, despite there being much opposition in these names, which is easy even for the very dull-witted to know. For it is clear that the only-begotten, if he truly be only-begotten, can no longer be firstborn, and the firstborn, as firstborn, cannot be only-begotten.
Therefore, if he is indeed the 'firstborn' of 'all creation,' and 'in him all things were created,' it is fitting for us to know that the apostle now remembers his economy according to the flesh.
Thus, he was named 'firstborn' of 'all creation' because of his birth according to the flesh, not because of the first creation, as they themselves think.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Creation of the Flesh
english: The body was able to attain such antiquity. But let one understand that even if it happens that the human flesh is most especially newer, yet the Word, having deemed it worthy to take this up through a pure virgin, having thus united it to himself, did not only labor tirelessly to create the man formed within himself as 'firstborn of all creation' (Col 1:15), but he also intends to be the beginning of all things, not of those on earth only, but also of those in the heavens.

Therefore, this main point of the Proverb (Prov 8:22) is not intended to present the beginning of the divinity of our Savior, as they themselves think, saying 'the Lord created me,' but the second economy according to the flesh; for this reason he mentions creation as a convenient way of referring to the human flesh. Surely the creation differs in its actual matter regarding his [being] according to man. Therefore he says, 'the Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works'; [he says] 'created me' clearly through the virgin Mary, through whom God intended to unite the human flesh to his own Word.

Because of this, then, having it thus, it is following to observe with the mind that main point of the Proverb said in this way: 'the Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works' (Prov 8:22). For our Lord God, the Master, having created what was not, has brought it into being; for the flesh, which the Word took up, was not existing, but rather, not existing, 'he created the beginning of his ways.' So then, fittingly, since the ancient things have passed away and new things are going to be, all through the newness of our Savior, our Lord Christ cried out through the prophet saying, 'the Lord created me as the beginning of his ways for his works' (Prov 8:22).

For this has become to us, those of us who are about to live justly in godliness, a way; the beginning of all the ways following these. And he has appropriately said 'beginning' and 'ways' concerning the Lord our Savior, because even of the other ways, which we have possessed, after the first way, a beginning has become, the traditions made manifest through the holy apostles of the 'from on high,' according to the prophecy, having preached to us this new mystery of 'proclamation.' 'He therefore created me,' he says, 'as the beginning of his ways for his works' (Prov 8:22). And what works does he say? Concerning which the Savior says, 'my Father is working until now, and I am working' (John 4:34), and again he says, 'the work,' 'I have finished what you gave me to do' (John 17:4).

For who could have believed, before the demonstration of the things, that the Word, having been begotten through a virgin, would take up our flesh and bodily demonstrate the whole deity in it? (16) 'Before the age he founded me,' calling this a foundation, refers to the economy predestined according to his flesh. (17) As also the apostle says, 'for no one can lay another foundation except that which is laid, which is Jesus Christ' (1 Corinthians 3:11). And of one age he mentions here, from which he said the things concerning Christ were to be founded, even though many ages have passed, as David said, 'the one existing before the ages' (Psalm 90:2). (17) For since Asterius has said that the Word came into being before the ages, the very words themselves refute him as lying; so as to protest not only the matter, but also the letter. (18) For if Proverbs says, 'before the age he founded me' (Proverbs 8:23), how did he say that he himself had come into being before the ages? For it is one thing to be founded before the age, and another to have come into being before the ages.

Just as the Pantokrator God predestined the church of old, (19) so also the economy according to the flesh of Christ, through whom he predestined to call the race of the God-fearing 'unto adoption of sonship,' having previously founded it in his own thought. (19) Because of this, the apostle clearly pre-announces by the Holy Spirit 'the predestined Son of God,' saying. (20) Surely, if even a mystery most new has appeared at the end of times, such that because of this it was predestined before this age, it is fitting that the prophet said, 'before the age he founded me,' making clear the flesh, because of the communion with the Word, his true Son. (21)

Then he says, 'in the beginning,' 'before making the earth' (Genesis 1:1). What earth, this one? Meaning our flesh, the earth which becomes again after the disobedience. (21) For 'earth' he says, 'I am,' and 'and into earth I shall depart' (Genesis 3:19). For it was necessary for this to receive healing, having shared in some way with the Holy Word. (22) Then he says, 'before making the abysses' (Psalm 36:9); here the prophet proverbially says the abysses are the hearts of the saints, those having the gift of the Spirit in their own depth. (23)

What then is this main point, 'before the springs of the waters came forth' (Psalm 36:9)? He says they are the holy apostles. (23) And this mystery presents to us the scripture of Exodus, pre-announcing long ago the types of the apostles. (24) For twelve...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Twelve Springs and the Star
english: Regarding the number of the apostles, twelve springs are remembered. Thus, concerning the fleshly generation, the Lord spoke through the prophet Solomon, saying, 'before the springs of the waters came forth' (Ps 89:9). Likewise, the Savior said toward the holy springs, 'having gone, make disciples of all nations' (Matt 28:19). It is evident from everywhere that the holy apostles and springs were tropically named by the prophet. Since we have spoken about those that went before, it follows to fill up the remainder. The remainder concerns the mountains and the hills. For he says, 'before the mountain was established' (Ps 132:6), and 'before all the hills, I beget you' (Ps 132:5). He calls the apostles and the successors of the apostles mountains and hills, so that the just administration concerning them might be indicated proverbially among other men.

Therefore, it seems to me that it is good to pass through even those things which we have not yet previously passed through. For most of those written by him have become clear to us from those already mentioned to us. 'From the womb,' he says, 'before the Morning Star, I begat you' (Ps 71:6), instead of 'I brought you forth'; for he thought that someone, having stolen the intention, would join in with the opinion of the heresy. Therefore, regarding the most important matter, having removed the syllable 'ex', he wished to indicate his ancient rebirth.

How then do those who are 'full of guile and fraudulence' (1 Tim 4:2), to speak apostolically, transfer the word to his first, as they think, creation, even though David clearly spoke this concerning his fleshly generation? For since darkness existed previously through the ignorance of godliness, he appropriately names the Morning Star after the day that is about to shine ('I am,' he says, 'the day' [Ps 110:3]). Therefore, because the Morning Star, who makes the day manifest, was so named by the prophet David, it is no longer right to seek who this Morning Star is, whoever he may be; for he was the star that appeared most recently, both bringing and declaring the day to the magi.

It is therefore evident that the phrase 'I begot you before the morning star' [Rev 22:16], spoken by the Pantokrator regarding the Word being born with human flesh through the Virgin, clearly signifies this of the Gospel: first, that our Lord was produced through the Virgin, and later, that the star which indicates the day appeared. For where else from the divine utterances can we find written that one is unbegotten and one is begotten in this way, as they themselves believed him to have been begotten; neither have prophets, evangelists, or apostles said this?

Therefore, the holy apostle and disciple of the Lord, John, remembering his simplicity, became a true witness of the Word, saying, 'In the beginning was the Word' [John 1:1], 'and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' [John 1:1]. Not mentioning any beginning of the Word there, but using three alternating testimonies, he established that the Word was in the beginning. I will remind you of what he himself wrote, presenting it to those written badly by Eusebius, so that you may know it clearly stands apart from the former promise. For he wrote to them in these words: the main point of the epistle is to bring forward the will of the Father regarding the generation of the Son, and not to let the birth of God appear as a passion. This is what the wisest of the fathers declared in their local compositions, guarding against the impiety of the heretics, who, setting forth dogmas, falsely judged the Godhead's childbearing to be something physical and passional.

Thus, Asterius, wishing to sympathize with Eusebius who wrote badly, by mentioning the nature of the Father and the nature of the unbegotten, has himself become his own accuser. For it was much better for the depth of Eusebius's meaning, as he himself wrote, to be left unexamined lying in brevity, than to use such a theory to bring the craftiness of the letter into the light. To say that he was begotten before the ages seems to follow; for an offspring comes from the one preceding it as a father. But regarding the other matter, he has not responded to it healthily or piously. For to not say that the one proceeding from him is the Word, and that this is the true manner of the generation, but merely a son, seems to provide some to those hearing a human perspective.

Paulinus did not write these things reminding of evangelical teaching, but confessing that some move thus from themselves, and some have this manner from the readings of the aforementioned men. Then finally, as if bringing a crown to the proof, he himself subscripted from the original words in his letter,
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Critique of Origen's Trinitarianism
english: Rather, it is possible to convince [others] by the evangelists and the apostles. And these are the spoken words: having repeated [the formula] concerning Father and Son and Holy Spirit, a few of those left from that time are to be set forth; concerning the Father, as being undivided and without division, he becomes Father of the Son, not putting him forth, as some suppose. For if the Son of the Father is a thing put forth and a generation from him, like the generations of living creatures, it is necessary for the one putting forth and the one being put forth to be a body.

Origen wrote these things, not desiring to learn the simplicity of the word from the holy prophets and apostles, but daring to narrate a second hypothesis of the word, having given it to himself. For that Origen writes such things using his own dogmas is evident from which he also many times overturns his own [teachings]. In another passage where he speaks concerning God, it is necessary to remind [the reader].

And he writes thus: For God the Father did not begin to be a father being hindered, as men who become fathers are, by the fact of not being able to be fathers yet. For if God is always perfect, and there is in him the power to be himself Father, and to be a good Father of such a Son, why is it necessary for him to cast himself down and to make himself secure, and, so to speak, as it is possible to be Father, does he not become Father? The same thing, however, must be said concerning the Holy Spirit.

How then, after Origen had written even this, did the blessed Paulinus, according to him, consider it not dangerous to conceal this, but to use it for the construction of what seemed right to him against the opponents, whose argument I would not say even Origen could be able to refute? And Paulinus, being persuaded by these spoken words and by this man's father, is not hesitant to say and to write the same things, sometimes calling Christ a second god and this one having become a more human god, sometimes defining him to be a creature. For he held that Christ is a creature, even towards us, when pursuing [the heretics] at Ancyra.

And because of this, he does not call himself the Son of God, but everywhere he calls himself the Son of Man, so that through such a confession he might prepare the man to become a son of God through the fellowship with him, and after the end of the work, again, as the Word, he might be united with God, fulfilling that which was foretold by the apostle: 'then he himself will subject to him all things who have subjected all things to him, so that God may be all and in all' (1 Cor 15:28). For it will be like what it was before.

For the Word 'was in the beginning' (John 1:1) was nothing other than the Word. But the man having been united to the Word, who was not previously, has become [a man] as John teaches us, saying, 'and the Word became flesh' (John 1:14). Therefore, it seems he mentions only the Word, whether the divine Scripture mentions the name of Jesus or Christ, appearing to name the Word of God who is after the flesh of the human. And if anyone promises to be able to show the name of Christ or Jesus solely upon the Word before the new covenant, he will find this said prophetically, as is also clear from this: 'the kings of the earth and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against His Christ' (Acts 4:26).

So it is evident from every side that it is not fitting to fit any name other than that which the most holy disciple and apostle of the Lord, John, said at the beginning of the Gospel, due to the simplicity of the Word. Since Christ and Jesus are preached after the ascension of the flesh, and [as] life and the way and the day and the resurrection and the door and the bread (John 14:6), if anything else were named by the divine [Scriptures], it does not befit us to ignore the first name, that he was the Word. For this reason also the most holy evangelist and disciple of the Lord, being very awake in the spirit, remembering the beginning from above and nothing newer, said, 'In the beginning was the Word' (John 1:1), and 'the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1), in order that he might show that if there is a new and newer name, it is from the new economy of Him according to the flesh.

For Sabellius himself, having slipped from the right faith, knew neither God accurately nor His holy Word. For he who did not know the Word ignored also the Father. For he says, 'no one knows the Father except the Son' (John 1:18), that is, the Word; for the Word provides the knowledge of the Father through himself. In this way also toward those who claim to know God like the Jews, while rejecting His Word, through whom...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Logos before and after Incarnation
english: God is known only [through the Son]; He said, "No one knows the Father except the Son, and whomever the Son shall reveal to Him" (Matthew 11:27). For since it was impossible to know God in any other way, He teaches men to know Him through His own Word, so that even he [the critic] fails to know accurately the Father and the Word of the latter. Therefore, let one learn that the Word of God has come—not a word named improperly, as they claim, but a Word existing truly.

It is not a word named improperly, even if those teaching falsely tear [the truth] apart by lying, but a Word existing principally and truly. [...] Among those teaching them, as if ashamed to remember the Word, which in this way all divine Scriptures proclaim. For David says about Him, "By the word of the Lord the heavens were established" (Psalm 8:3), and again, "He sent out His word and healed them" (Psalm 18:1). And Solomon says, "Evil men will seek me, and will not find me. For they hated wisdom, and did not choose the word of the Lord" (Proverbs 8:12). And Isaiah says, "For out of Zion shall go forth [the law], and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem" (Isaiah 2:3). And again Jeremiah says, "The wise have been defiled, and they have been foolish, and they have fallen, because they rejected the word of the Lord" (Jeremiah 23:29). And the prophet Hosea says, "They have hated [Him] in the gates while rebuking, and they have loathed a holy word" (Hosea 8:12). And Micah similarly, remembering the Word, says, "Out of Zion shall go forth law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem" (Micah 4:2).

Indeed, before the descent and being born of a virgin, there was only the Word. For what else was there before the one who descended "in the last days" (Hebrews 1:2), and having been born of a virgin, took upon himself flesh? There was nothing else but the Word.

It is quite so, then, that before the descent this was [the case], as we have often said: the Word. But after the descent and the assumption of flesh, it has encountered various objections, since "the Word became flesh" (John 1:14).

For what other mystery was hidden than that concerning the Word? It was thus hidden 'in God'; this mystery was prior, so that no one of the former people was to know clearly the things concerning the Word, but we now enjoy the wealth of 'the glory' and the hidden mystery.

The holy apostle John, both disciple and student of the Lord, clearly and explicitly teaches at the beginning of the Gospel, as something previously unknown among men, naming it the Word of the Pantokrator, thus saying, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). He employs more than one witness to signify the eternity of the Word. In saying 'In the beginning was the Word', he shows by power that the Word is in the Father (for God is the beginning of all things 'from whom all things [are]') [cf. Rom 11:36]; and in 'and the Word was with God', he shows the Word to be with God in activity ('for all things were made through him, and without him not one thing was made' [John 1:3]); and in 'the Word was God', he says not to divide the divinity, since the Word is in Him and He is in the Word; for he says, 'the Father is in me, and I in the Father' (John 14:10).

Thus you hear the harmony of the Holy Spirit, testifying to the eternity of the Word through many and diverse persons. Because of this, he begins from the eternity of the Word, saying 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God' (John 1:1). Using three successive witnesses, he intends to demonstrate the eternity of the Word.

What then was this thing that descended before the incarnation? He says certainly: a spirit. For if he wished to say anything other than this, the angel who spoke to the virgin would not permit him, saying 'the Holy Spirit will come upon you' (Luke 1:35). But if he says it is a spirit, let him hear the Savior saying 'Spirit is God' (1 John 5:20). Yet it seems that the Father is in the Word, even if it does not seem so to Asterius and to those who think the same as him. For this seems to the prophetic prophet Isaiah,
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Divine Logos and Creation
english: Regarding the one saying through the Holy Spirit, 'and they shall worship you, and in you they shall pray; for in you is God, and there is no other besides you. For you are God' (Rev 22:8), you see how he uproots the skillful cunning of those teaching falsely. Likewise, there the prophet discourses about the Word having taken our flesh. A spirit of shadow could never have become a creative spirit. And because he is God himself, the Savior said, 'Spirit, God' (John 1:1). And because God is light, he himself teaches us, saying, 'I am the light' (John 8:12).

For who else, whether of the holy angels or of righteous men, was reliable enough to loose the penalty set for him from the face of God, if not the Word himself, who is both co-existing and co-forming, toward whom the Father said, 'Let us make man in our image and likeness' (Gen 1:26), with no other god existing who would be able to co-form with him? 'I am,' he says, 'the first God, and I after these things, and besides me no other god exists.' Nor was there any younger god, nor was any other god being 'after these things' able to work together with God.

But if anyone uses a small and human example like ours to examine the divine action as if through an icon: just as a skilled man who is a statue-maker, desiring to fashion a man, first observes his forms and characters within himself, then conceives what breadth and length is becoming, and examines the proportion of the whole in each individual part, having prepared the appropriate material of bronze, and having modeled the coming man after his own intellect and seeing him mentally, consciously cooperating with the Logos—by which he reasons and by which he is accustomed to do all things (for nothing beautiful comes into being without the Logos)—beginning this sensible work, he exhorts himself as if to another, saying, 'Come, let us make, come, let us fashion a man';

Thus the Lord of all, God, making the ensouled man from the earth, exhorts no one else but his own Logos, saying, 'Let us make man' (Gen 1:26), not in the same way as the others; for the whole creation came into being by the Logos. For God did not need any other preparation, such as matter or some other human thing, but this preparation which is in his own intellect.

Since it was impossible to conceive of God apart from the Word and the wisdom approaching the Word regarding the construction of the heavens, he rightly said, 'Whenever he was preparing the heavens, I was with him' (Proverbs 8:30). For before the world existed, the Word was in the Father. When the Almighty God set to make all things in the heavens and upon the earth, the genesis of the world required an active energy. And because of this, with no other existing besides God (for all is confessed to have come from him), the Word, having come forth, became the maker of the world, he who previously was inwardly preparing it, just as the prophet Solomon teaches us, saying, 'Whenever he was preparing the heavens, I was with him' (Proverbs 8:30) and 'As he was establishing springs under the heavens, whenever he was making the strong foundations of the earth, I was with him, fittingly joined to him; I was there as he was being applied' (Proverbs 8:29). For the Father rightly rejoiced in making all things through the Word with wisdom and power.

Just as all things that happened came from the Father through the Word, so also the things said by the Father are signified through the Word. For this reason also the most holy Moses names the Word an angel there, because he appeared through no other, but so that he might announce to Moses those things which he knew would be effective for the sons of Israel; and he knew they would be effective for believing that there is one God. Therefore also to him he said, 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14), in order that he might teach that no other besides himself is God. This is easy, I think, for those thinking well to know from a small and humble example among us. For it is not possible for anyone to separate the word of a man in power and substance; for the word is one and the same to a man, and is not separated from anything else, except by the energy of the act alone.

Here the Father says 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14) to Moses, but he says it clearly through the Word. For all that the Father says, he seems to be saying everywhere through the Word. And this is clear also from ourselves, in whatever small things we compare to the great and divine; for we also do all that we wish to say and do through our own word, according to our ability.

What then, does Asterios suppose the one saying 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14) to be, the Son or the Father? For two substances, setting aside the one which the Word of God took flesh into, the human one, and [...]
