title: The Distinction of Hypostases
english: By imagining him thus, he calls the Father and the Son to be such, thereby separating the Son of God from the Father, just as anyone would separate a son of a man from his father according to nature. If he is said to have spoken these things to Moses while separating the Father from himself as the Son, he will not confess the Son to be God. For how can he allow the one saying 'I am the Being' (Exodus 3:14) not to agree that the Being says he is in opposition to non-being? But if he would posit the Son as being separated, he would be said to say 'I am the Being' regarding the Father as well. Either of these is impious.

Therefore, I shall begin to oppose each of those who have written incorrectly, starting from the epistle written by him. He wrote to believe in the Father as God the Almighty, and in his Son the only-begotten God, the Lord our Jesus Christ, and in the Holy Spirit; and he says that he has learned this way of godliness from the divine writings. And I, when he says this, accept the things said very much, for this is the common way of godliness for all of us, to believe in the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit; but when, not having considered the divine, he says the Father is Father and the Son is Son more humanly to us through some technical theory, one can no longer praise such a theory as harmless. For through such a theory, the heresy currently conceived by them comes to increase, which I think is easy to demonstrate clearly from his own words. For he said that one must believe the Father to be truly Father and the Son truly Son, and the Holy Spirit likewise.

For it is impossible for three hypostases to be one unity, unless the Trinity first has its beginning from a unity. For the holy Paul said that those things are being recapitulated into a unity, which differ from God in nothing regarding unity; for the Word and the Spirit alone differ from God in unity.

If, therefore, the Word seems to have come forth from the Father and come to us, and the Holy Spirit, as Asterius also confessed, proceeds from the Father, the Savior immediately says concerning the Spirit that 'he will not speak of himself, but whatever he hears he will speak, and he will declare to you the things that are coming' (John 16:13).

"He shall take from mine and he will announce to you" (John 16:5), the monad does not appear here clearly and manifestly, but in a secret word, expanding into a trinity yet by no means undergoing division. For if the Word proceeds from the Father, and the Spirit also is confessed to proceed from the Father, and immediately regarding the Spirit the Savior says, "He shall take from mine and he will announce to you" (John 16:5), is it not then evident that a mystery is being hidden to be revealed? For how, if the monad being undivided were not expanding into a trinity, could it contain him regarding the Spirit to say at times that he proceeds from the Father, and at times to say, "He shall take from mine and he will announce to you" (John 16:5), and immediately after having breathed upon the disciples, "Receive Holy Spirit" (John 20:22) having said?

For how, if he proceeds from the Father, does he promise to receive this ministry from the Son? For it is necessary either that, being divided into two, as Asterius said, there be persons, or that the Spirit proceeding from the Father must not be in need of the ministry from the Son (for everything proceeding from the Father must be perfect, by no means being dependent on the help of another), or, if he receives from the Son and by his power ministers the grace, he no longer proceeds from the Father. If, however, the Gospel said that having breathed upon the disciples, "Receive Holy Spirit" (John 20:22), he had said, it is evident that the Spirit came forth from the Word. How then, if the Spirit proceeded from the Word, does it again proceed from the Father?

Therefore, he has not spoken correctly nor appropriately, having said that there are three hypostases, not once, but a second time. We know the economy according to the flesh to differ for the man, but we have believed the incorcorporeality according to the spirit to be united to the Father. For if the examination of the Spirit were the only one, it would seem fitting that the Word be one and the same with God; but if the addition according to the flesh upon the Savior were being examined, it seems that the divinity is being expanded by energy alone, so that it would seem fitting that the monad truly is undivided.

For Asterius had decided that there are one and the same, according to this, only the Father and the Son, in accordance with which they agree in all things. For so he said: and because of the precise [account] in all words and works...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Harmony of the Son and Father
english: Regarding the harmony of 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). If, therefore, He himself says these things: 'I went forth from the Father and I have come,' and again, 'and the Word, which you hear, is not mine, but belongs to Him who sent me the Father,' and 'all things that the Father has are mine' (John 16:15), it is clear that He was rightly saying even that: 'the Father is in me and I in the Father' (John 16:33), so that the Word, saying this, might be in God, and the Father might be in the Word, because the Word is the power of the Father. For a trustworthy witness has declared Him to be 'the power of God and the wisdom of God.'

The Savior does not say 'I and the Father are one' because of a precise harmony in all words and works, as Asterius said, but because it is impossible to divide the Word of God or God Himself from the Word. Since Asterius thinks the Savior said this because of a harmony in everything, and desires to learn the truth without paying attention to the second economy, it is necessary to remind him how, at times, one sees what appears to be a discord. For such is what the spoken words teach us.

For what kind of harmony is there in the time of the passion when He says this, 'Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me' (Luke 22:42), but then adds that, 'yet not as I will, but as You' (Luke 22:42)? For there was no harmony at first in saying, 'let this cup pass from me'; nor does it seem that there is any agreement in what is being added, for He says, 'not my will, but Yours, Father, let it be done.' You hear how the letter declares a discord, according to appearances, of the one willing and of the one not willing. For the Father clearly willed that which willed happened through the things from which it was clear; but the Son's not willing is made clear through the things by which He renounces it. And again He says, 'I do not seek my own will, but the will of Him who sent me the Father' (John 5:30). How, then, does he say that the Savior said, 'I and the Father are one' because of a harmony in everything?

How can the Son have harmony toward the Father, or the Father toward the Son, when the Son says, 'all things that the Father has are mine' (John 16:15)? For, contrary to the Son encroaching upon the Father, he says, 'all things that the Father has are mine.' For this reason, passing over the fact that all things the Father has are common, he said, 'all things that the Father has are mine.'

Even if it was not proper for the one in agreement to speak in this way, rather: all that the Father has is common. For if the Acts of the Apostles, praising the agreement of those approaching with faith like the ones mentioned, said, "all things were common to them" (Acts 4:32), and one ought to consider all things to be common for men capable of agreeing, how much more ought the Father and the Son to partake in communion, being divided into two hypostases?

But now, in saying, "all that the Father has is mine" (John 16:15), the Son seems to be grasping at the Father's; and in stating that not even his own word is master, but rather the Father of this [word] (for he says, "the word which you hear is not mine but of Him who sent me, the Father" [John 8:28]), it shows the Father being deprived of his own things of the Son. Furthermore, according to the opinion of Asterius, the two sides seem not to have spoken in accordance. For the one in agreement ought not to justly snatch away what belongs to the other, for this is grasping, but ought to consider what belongs to each to be common.

So when we look down toward the flesh in a human way, we will not find the Savior having said, "I and the Father are one" (John 10:30), just as Asterius has written. For it was not because of the precise agreement in all words and works, as he himself has written, that the Savior said, "I and the Father are one." For if it were this, he certainly would have said: "I and the Father agree with one another in all things." But now he said, "I and the Father are one."

So if there were any disagreement in those [things], and since the Lord must speak the truth, it is fitting to know the Savior precisely, that whenever he says, "I and the Father are one," he says this not looking down toward the man whom he took upon himself, but toward the Word proceeding from the Father. For if any disagreement were thought to exist, this ought to be referred to the weakness of the flesh, which the Word did not have previously when he was taken. But if unity were being spoken of, this seems to differ from the Word. Therefore, not only did he say, "I and the Father are one" appropriately, but also that: "For such a long time I have been with you, Philip, and you say: show me the Father" (John 14:9), it is clear that [he said this] for those capable of seeing the intelligible things not with these eyes, but with the intellectual ones. For both the Father and his Word exist invisible to the eyes of the flesh. Therefore, not because of the agreement in all things...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unity of Christ's Divinity
english: He spoke to Philip. For he himself confesses, saying, "The Father is in me, and I am in the Father" (John 14:10). That he has not spoken this merely or aimlessly is evident also from another apostolic saying: "one" is he who said, "one Lord, one faith, one baptism" (Ephesians 4:5), and "one God" he said, "and Father, who is over all and through all and in all" (1 Corinthians 8:6). You see that the concord does not fail even there, but the same thing has suffered even there. For having said "one Lord," he again said "one God," so that whenever he mentions the one Lord, he includes the Father, and whenever he speaks concerning the Father, he testifies that the Word is not outside Him.

If you wish to hear something else of the same prophecy confirming one God for us, he says, "I am God first, and I am the one who is to come" (Isaiah 43:10). For the "I" is indicative of a single person, for the two sayings signify one person to us. For having said "I," the "am" follows, so that through these two parts of the word, both the pronoun and the verb, the unity of the divinity is testified. If other testimony were required, I would immediately provide you with the same prophet saying, "I am first, and I am after these things, and besides me there is no God" (Isaiah 45:5).

If Asterius, having supposed the Son of the Father to be divided, assumes him to be a son of a man, being stumbled by the human flesh which He took for our sakes, let him show us this saying; for the said saying is of one person even there. Who then is he who says, "There is no God besides me"? Let him hear also another prophecy saying, "There is no just one and savior besides me" (Isaiah 43:11).

If it is thought that there are two gods, it is necessary for him to confess that the other is not just, nor a savior. But if he is not just nor a savior, how can he still be God? For he appears to be the one who is just and a savior.

And again he says, 'Before me no other came, and with me no other shall be; I am God, and no savior shall be besides me.' If one wishes to hear another prophetic word, perhaps regarding him and those similarly disputing about divinity as he spoke, let him hear Isaiah saying, 'Repent, you wanderers, turn to the heart, and remember the former things from eternity, for I am God and there is none besides me' (Isaiah 43:10). He did not say, 'I am God,' so that he might clearly demonstrate a single God existing through the addition of the article.

And what of the prophet Hosea? Does he not himself testify to the same things, saying, 'I brought you up out of Egypt' and 'you shall know no god besides me, and no savior is besides me' (Hosea 13:4)? And again Malachi says, 'Did not one God create you?' and 'Is not one Father of all you?' (Malachi 2:10). But Asterios will say that David said nothing about this, even though being older than the other prophets according to Moses, and because of this he is in doubt, whether it is proper to suppose two gods existing as divided substances or not.

I think, however, that in order not to say this, it would follow for him to show him the same things with the aforementioned holy ones saying: 'Listen,' he says, 'my people, and I will speak to you; Israel, and I testify to you. If you listen to me, there shall not be among you a near god, nor shall you worship a foreign god. For I am the Lord your God.' In demonstrating himself and saying, 'I am,' is it not clear that he is saying there is only one God, that is, himself?

What then? If we do not consider the unity to be indivisible by power through the Spirit, shall we not sin, clearly being taught by the word, 'You shall worship the Lord your God and to him alone you shall serve'? The same is also proclaimed through the Gospel according to Mark; for a certain scribe having come to him and inquiring what is the first of the commandments, he answered him thus, having said, 'First of all: Hear, Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one, and you shall love the Lord your God with all your...'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Unity of God in Scripture
english: ...of your soul and with all your strength. This is the first; and the second is like unto this: you shall love your neighbor as yourself (Mark 12:30-31). Greater than these no other commandment exists. And the scribe said to him: 'Well, Teacher, in truth you have spoken, that one is the God and there is none other besides him' (Mark 12:32-33). But the scribe, seeming to have learned piety through the law, appears to be praising the explicit word of the Savior: 'Hear, O Israel' (Deuteronomy 6:4), saying, 'the Lord our God is one,' and believing that he has spoken well by an oath; for he says, 'in truth you have spoken that one is the God and there is no other besides him.'

But those who follow the new covenant, desiring to know mysteries, these also wish to reconstruct a god, wanting to separate him by substance and power from the Father. For the divine Scripture knows to call the unity Lord and God; it has already become clear from the things previously mentioned, through which the God said to Moses, his own servant: 'And God spoke again to Moses: Thus you shall say to the sons of Israel: The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham and the God of Isaac and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you' (Exodus 3:6).

You see how, by demonstrating one thing here, he addresses the same person as Lord and God. And immediately likewise the Scripture says, 'And the Lord spoke all these words, saying: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery. There shall not be to you other gods besides me' (Exodus 20:2-3); you hear how through the pronoun it is made apparent that there is only one God. And again a little later he says, 'I am the Lord your God,' saying that he himself is Lord and God.

And what else do we learn through other Scripture? 'And you shall know this day,' he says, 'and your mind shall not be diverted, that the Lord your God, this is God in the heaven above and upon the earth below, and there is none besides him' (Deuteronomy 4:39). And again in the same Deuteronomy he says, 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; and you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind' (Deuteronomy 6:4-5). And again in the same: 'Behold, behold that I am, and there is no God besides me; I will kill and I will make live; I will strike and I will heal' (Deuteronomy 32:39).

How then, pretending to follow the holy Scriptures simply and boldly, Asterius did not recognize this part of the saying: "The Lord your God, this is God in the heaven above and upon the earth below, and there is none other besides him" (Deuteronomy 6:4), and that "He is one" and "there is no other besides him"?

How then will the holy prophet Jeremiah not clearly expose him as teaching a different doctrine? For he, prophesying to us according to the Savior, thus said: "This is our God; another shall not be reckoned against him. He found every way of knowledge, and he gave Jacob to his child and Israel to the one beloved by him. After these things he appeared upon the earth, and he associated himself with men" (Jeremiah 24:7).

So that even if someone says, by first constructing a first god and a second, as Narcissus has written with those words (for even he who says, "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness" [Genesis 1:26], does not forgive), that both he himself and his father are two, we have heard this in part from the testimony of the Lord and of the holy Scriptures. If, therefore, Narcissus intends to divide the Word of the Father through this, let him know that the prophet who wrote, speaking as if of God, "Let us make man in our image and after our likeness," himself wrote, "And God made the man" (Genesis 1:27).

For having encountered the letter of Narcissus, the leader of the Neronians, which he wrote to one Christian and to Euphronius and Eusebius, as the Holy Bishop had asked him whether he says the same as Eusebius of the two substances of Palestine, I knew from what was written that he believes there are three substances, while answering. For having dared to divide the Word of God and to name another god the Word, and having divided the substance and the power of the Father, it is easy to learn clearly from the very words written by them into what blasphemy he has fallen. For he wrote with those words thus: the image and that of which the image is are not conceived as one and the same, but rather two substances and two things and two powers, as are so many distinctions. But the Apostle writes such things concerning the faith of the Galatians; yet Eusebius, transferring the apostolic meaning, through which the Apostle, on account of the aforementioned reason, said, "My children, whom I again labor with until Christ is formed in you" (Galatians 4:19), fastened down the Galatians as not having the correct view concerning the glory of God. For he truly labored with a certain sharpness...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Error of Asterius regarding Eusebius
english: And a bitter pain, because he believed the Galatians regarding godliness to be not as that man was boasting, nor even two substances, but that things and powers and gods were being spoken of. Thus also Eusebius of Caesarea has written, having the same glory for both Paul and those from the outside regarding gods. For he wrote not as if there were only one god, but as there is one of the only true God. Therefore, having learned, Asterius's father Paulinus thought that there were newer gods.

How then did these, having turned to the same worst path as those from the outside, intend to teach and write the same things, as Eusebius spoke similarly to Valentinus and Hermas, and Narcissus to Marcian and Plato? But having set aside the true knowledge, he provided for us an artful system and now has demonstrated a theory. For not having the will to construct his own from the divine writings, he rushes upon the wisest, as he thinks, a father claiming; which the wisest of the fathers in their own local arrangements have decided.

Asterius says that his father has decided upon a resolution and has written a dogma regarding God from their own choice. For the name of dogma has the character of human will and opinion. And that this is so, the dogmatic art of the physicians testifies sufficiently to us, and the so-called dogmas of the philosophers also testify; and that even those things which seemed to be in agreement are still called dogmas of agreement, I think no one is ignorant of.

For having wished to sympathize with Eusebius, who wrote the letter badly, he said, first of all, not having developed the dogma teaching-wise, that he arranged the letter; for the letter was not made for the church nor for those who are ignorant, but for the blessed Paulinus, having said blessed him for this reason, that he had the same glory as Asterius. Since we have learned that the wisest of the fathers are Asterius's, I think it follows to say that he became a teacher of both Paulinus and the others. For from the letter of Paulinus, he having become his teacher would have been evident to us.

Even if it is necessary to speak the truth about Origen, it is fitting to say this: that he, having lately turned away from the studies according to philosophy and having preferred to converse with the divine through words before the precise grasp of the Scriptures, began to write by preferring the much and ambitious external education to that which is necessary; he was provided with words by those of philosophy, and through them he did not write well. It is evident; for he, still remembering the dogmas of Plato and the difference regarding the principles with him, wrote a book 'On Principles' and placed this as the title upon the treatise. A greatest example of this is that he made the beginning of the words from nothing other than the title of the book, but from the sayings spoken by Plato; for he wrote beginning thus: 'Those who have believed and have been persuaded.' This spoken thing, having been said thus, one would find in Plato's Gorgias.

And I deem it worthy of those encountering the holy [writings], having truly received seeds and principles of this explanation, to add more proofs to those things said, so that even more the predispositions of those turning away from the faith might be checked. For truly, the God who begat them 'left them, and they dug for themselves broken cisterns' (Jeremiah 2:13).

I think it follows to speak briefly and concerning the icon. For he wrote: 'Another is he who was born from him, who is the icon of the invisible God' (Colossians 1:15). Because of this 'icon,' Asterius remembers the invisible God, in order to teach how much the God of the Word differs, just as a man seems to differ from his own icon.

Because of this, it is appropriate that he brings forward 'who is the icon of the invisible God.' When did he become an icon, or how long did he take 'according to icon and according to likeness' as a form? For previously, as I have often said, he was nothing other than the Word. Is it not therefore evident that before the assumption of our body, the Word in himself was not an icon of the invisible God? For it is fitting to see an icon, so that through the icon the entirely unseen might be able to be seen. How then has Asterius written that the Word of God is an icon of the invisible God? For icons of those things which are icons are also indicative of the absent, so that even the absent seems to appear through them. But if it happens that the Word is invisible while the invisible God exists, how can the Word be an icon of the invisible God, being himself invisible? For it is impossible for the unseen to [be seen] through the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Icon of the Invisible God
english: The invisible is sometimes shown. Therefore, it is clear from everywhere that the icon of the invisible God was spoken by the Apostle as that which became flesh through the Word, so that through the visible the invisible might be shown. For the Apostle says, 'the icon is of the invisible God.' Now, clearly, having become according to the icon of God, the one who took up the form was received as flesh, and has become a true icon of the invisible God.

For if through this icon we were worthy to know the Word of God, we ought to believe Him, the Word, through the icon, saying, 'I and the Father are one' (John 10:30). For neither the Word nor the Father of the Word can be known in any way without this icon. Thus also the Apostle says, as we said a little earlier, 'he emptied himself, having taken the form of a servant' (Phil 2:7), signifying to us the human flesh through the form of a servant, which our Lord God, by His own spreading wisdom, said, 'let us make man in our icon and likeness' (Gen 1:26), rightly naming the human flesh an icon. For He knew precisely that an icon would be a little later than His own Word.

What then will he say regarding these things? For I do not think he has anything to say about this. Nor do I think he can clearly and persuasively confess to others that which he himself hides in his own mind, as being clearly to be learned from that which he has written. For another, he says, is the Father, who begat from himself the only-begotten Word and firstborn of all creation, alone alone, perfect of the perfect, king of kings, Lord of lords, God of God, an unchangeable icon of essence and will and power and glory.

These words clearly expose his faulty glory concerning divinity. For how can the Lord, having been begotten and being God, as He Himself previously said, be able to be an icon of God? For one thing is an icon of God, and another is God. So if [He is] an icon, [He is] neither Lord nor God, but an icon of Lord and God; but if [He is] truly Lord and God, then the Lord and God can no longer be an icon of Lord and God. Therefore, he does not intend for any of those things he has spoken to be [true]; for he says that he is an icon of all these things.

If, then, an image is of substance, it can no longer be the substance itself; and if it is an image of will, it can no longer be the will itself; and if it is an image of power, it is no longer power; and if it is an image of glory, it is no longer glory. For an image is an image not of itself, but of another.

Indeed, the matter concerning Asterius does not grieve us so much because such things were written, but because certain ones, appearing to be leaders of the church, neglecting the apostolic tradition and preferring external things, dared to write and teach such things, which possess no less error than those previously mentioned. It is necessary, then, to cry out to the Lord with tears and grief, saying, 'We have sinned, we have been impious, we have transgressed,' and 'we have done evil before you,' and now, having recognized this, we deem ourselves worthy to receive philanthropy from you. This was fitting for him, and it was appropriate to say these things because of the immeasurable goodness and philanthropy of God.

Even so, it was following to oppose a God who is cared for with philanthropy and justice, saying, 'If an enemy reproaches me, I would have been crushed if he had magnified himself against me. But you, O man, equal-souled, my leader and my knower, who sweetened my meals at the same time, we walked in the house of God in concord.' For we know from his own words that it was understood by his ministers: 'Behold,' for he said, 'I will be with you all the days of your life, even unto the end of the age.' Then, following this, he would have naturally added even the things that follow those that lead, 'Let death come upon them, and let them descend into Hades while living; for wickedness is in their hearts.' For the Scripture says that those who are in ignorance of impiety are being swallowed by Hades as dead; for they were dead, even though they seemed to live.

For they want the Savior to be a man; and it is evident from those things that Eusebius, through craftiness, turned the words of the apostle toward his own will. As one desiring to bring forth from some ancient great pain a most wicked slander, he 'poured out from his own treasure' the evil, according to the saying of the Savior. Desiring to show the Savior as a man only, thus uncovering for us the greatest secret mystery of the apostle, he said: therefore, the divine apostle most clearly cries out and has cried out the secret and mystical theology which he delivers to us, 'One is God,' and then, after the one God, he says...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Divinity of Christ vs Eusebius
english: "One mediator of God and men, a man, Christ Jesus." If therefore he says that he is a man, attending only to his administration according to the flesh, he certainly also confesses that thing, that there is no hope in him. For the prophet Jeremiah said, "Cursed is the man who has hope in man" (Jeremiah 17:5). But the one previously mentioned, having cared for the brevity of the holy prophets, as if explaining a certain secret and hidden theology of the apostle, said, "One God," he said, "one and mediator of God and men, a man, Christ Jesus." And he, having written these things and being very great regarding the remembering of the Scriptures, did not perceive that the most holy apostle, having written this, had written that: "Who, existing in the form of God, did not consider being equal to God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, having taken the form of a slave, becoming in the likeness of man and found in the appearance of a man" (Philippians 2:6-8).

Do you see how (as foretelling by the Spirit the malice of these) the holy apostle thus in another part wrote "as a man" and "becoming in the likeness of man," in order that he might stop their such great blasphemy. How then, not adhering to these things, does Eusebius alone intend for the Savior to be only a man? He is not daring to say this openly, but he is convicted by his expressions of wanting this.

For before the creation of all, there was a certain silence, as it were, existing in the God of the Word. For if Asterius believed the God to be the maker of all, it is evident that he himself will also confess to us that He is always existing, never having taken the beginning of being, and that the things that have come to be were made by Him and out of non-being. For I do not think he believes this too, that there is something and ungenerated, but rather is precisely convinced that both heaven and earth and all things existing in the heavens and upon the earth were brought into being by God.
If therefore this is believed, it is necessary for him to confess also that, besides God, there was nothing else. The Word possessed his own glory, being in the Father.

Asterius names the authority given to him as glory, and not glory only but also a glory pertaining to the world, not understanding that, lest anything else existed besides God alone, it was not from the world's becoming. For man has received not only authority over things on earth, but also of those in the heavens, appropriately; for if, when he became both 'man' and 'mediator of God and men' (1 Timothy 2:5), then 'all things were created' into him, as the apostle said, 'the things in heaven and those on earth' (Colossians 1:16), it is strictly following to know that authority is given to him not only of those on earth, but also of those in the heavens.

For if the holy Gospel says regarding a certain glory given to him by the Father, the man appears to have received this through the Word. For having become 'mediator of God and men' (1 Timothy 2:5) according to the holy apostle, he glorified God-fearing men by the glory given to him by the Father. And he enabled the fallen man, through disobedience, to be joined to himself through the Virgin by the Word. For what other greater glory could come among men than this glory? And having said 'I have glorified you' (John 17:22), he brings forth by saying 'and I will glorify again' (John 17:24), so that through an excess of philanthropy, by a second glory after the resurrection of the flesh, he might accomplish making the formerly mortal man immortal, and by such a glory glorifying him, so that not only might he be freed from the former slavery, but also might be worthy of a glory above man.

So that, as I said, having been previously deceived by the devil, he might prepare the man himself to conquer the devil again. Because of this, he took up the man, so that he might prepare him to receive following this an earnest of the authority. For this is the beloved, the man united to the Word, concerning whom the evangelist said, 'This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased' (Matthew 3:17). Because the Word of the invisible God through [...]
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Kingship of Christ through the Incarnation
english: It was destined that a virgin should give birth and that the human flesh should be taken up, so that through it, having overcome the devil who previously dominated man, He would not only make him incorruptible and immortal, but also a co-regent in the heavens with God. Indeed, having come down and having taken flesh through the virgin, He was established as king over the church, clearly so that through the Word, the man who had previously fallen from the kingship of the heavens might be able to attain kingship.

Therefore, God, desiring that this man—who previously fell from lordship due to disobedience—become Lord and God, worked out this economy. The most holy prophet David says prophetically, 'The Lord has reigned, let the earth rejoice' (Ps 96:1). For which reason, as if having received the beginning of kingship from a certain time of our Lord Christ, the prophecy says, 'But I have been made king by him' (Ps 2:6).

For this reason also, having become and reigning in human flesh, having established through the Word the man who was previously deceived as king, He 'will abolish all principality' (Col 2:15) of the devil 'and power and authority.' For it is said, 'it is necessary for him to reign' 'until he has placed the enemies under his feet' (1 Cor 15:25). This is the end of the kingship of our Lord Christ, says the holy apostle, to subject all things to his feet (1 Cor 15:28).

There, the apostle reveals a greatest mystery to us: that there would be an end, claiming it of Christ's kingship; but an end then, when he subjects all things under his feet. We have said in the discourses proceeding before us that our Lord Christ has had the beginning of kingship, using proofs from the divine writings. One says, 'But I have been made king by him upon Zion, his holy mountain' (Ps 2:6); another, 'The Lord has reigned, let the peoples be moved to wrath' (Ps 97:4); and again, 'The Lord has reigned, let the earth rejoice' (Ps 96:1). And it is possible to show with abundance myriads of words for testimony, that the man has received the beginning of kingship through the Word.

If, then, the kingdom began not more than four hundred years ago, it is nothing paradoxical, if the apostle says that he will deliver the kingdom which occurred so recently, meaning that he is a king whom God established, as the Scripture says. It seems that he is separated from the Father by energy alone because of the outward show of the flesh, until such time as the one approaching the judgment reveals the appointed time, so that the remaining part may follow, consequently, the pattern of those who were cast out after having seen the one who was cast out, as the prophecy says. For all are destined to be made subject to Christ in the time of the end, as the apostle said, just as 'he himself shall subject all things to him who subjected all things to him.'

What then do we learn concerning the human flesh, which the Word took not all years ago, but four hundred? Will the Word have this [flesh] also in the coming ages, or only until the time of the judgment? For what the prophet said must be confirmed in deed. For he says, 'they shall see him whom they cast out'; and they cast out, clearly, the flesh. For the Word did not take flesh so as to benefit our own self, but so that the flesh might attain immortality through communion with the Word, which is evident even from the Savior's own decision. Regarding the flesh, while possessing it and conversing with the disciples, he says thus: 'Does this scandalize you? If, then, you see the Son of Man departing from where he was previously; the Spirit gives life, the flesh profits nothing.'

If he confesses that the flesh profits him nothing, how can he allow the one existing from the earth, which profits nothing, to remain in the coming ages as being useful to the Word? For this is why it seems to me that even the Almighty God, the Lord, says to him, 'Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.' He seems to be separated by energy alone because of the human flesh, and as if defining a specific time for him of the seated position at the right hand, he says to him, 'until I make your enemies a footstool for your feet.'

This prophecy of David is made clearer to us by the holy apostle, who thus said: 'for he must reign until he makes his enemies a footstool of his feet.' Thus, both his human administration and his kingdom seem to have a limit. For he wills nothing other than what was said by the apostle: 'until he makes his enemies a footstool of his feet.'
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Economy of the Word and Restoration
english: So indeed, when the enemies have no longer a footstool under their feet in this part of the kingdom, he becomes king over all in general; for he co-reigns with 'God and Father', of whom the Word was and is. For the Word himself by himself has not taken the beginning of the kingdom, but the man deceived by the devil through the power of the Word has become king, so that having become king he might conquer the devil who previously deceived.

For this reason also the Acts of the Apostles concerning this man, whom the Word of God took and having taken sits at the right hand of the Father, teach in this way, saying, 'whom it is necessary to receive into heaven until the times of restoration' (Acts 1:11). And these, as if defining a certain boundary and a deadline in which it is fitting the economy according to man to be joined to the Word, say so. For what else does 'until the times of restoration' mean, except to signify to us an age to come, in which it is necessary for all things to attain the perfection of restoration?

If therefore in the time of the restoration of all things even the creation itself will be changed from slavery into freedom, as Paul said (for he says, 'because even the creation itself will be freed from the slavery of corruption into the freedom of the glory of the children of God' [Romans 8:21]), how could it still be possible for the Word to possess the form of a slave, which the Word took, as a form being a slave? Therefore, clearly and emphatically, in a brief time of both the past and the coming ages, the economy of the Word according to the flesh has happened for us, and Paul the lawgiver has declared that this shall have as both a beginning and an end, having said in this way, 'then the end, when he hands over the kingdom to God and Father' (1 Corinthians 15:24), referring to having grasped the human body and showing it to those seeing, 'does this scandalize you?'. He said, 'if therefore you see the Son of Man ascending, where was the former one? The spirit gives life, the flesh profits nothing' (John 6:63).

So indeed, not for himself, but for us the Word took human flesh. And if, having taken it, it appears through us, and all things concerning us will attain an end by his providence and energy at the time of judgment, there will no longer be a need even for this part of the kingdom.

But if anyone says that because of this the human flesh is worthy of the Word, because through the resurrection He fashioned it immortal, let him know that not everything that is immortal is worthy of God. For God is greater even than immortality itself, being able by His own will to make non-existent things immortal. It is clear that not all that is immortal is worthy of union with God, and it does not differ from this in the case of the beginning, the authorities, and the immortal angels. If anyone should inquire about this flesh, which has become immortal in the Word, what shall we say to him? We consider it not safe to dogmatize about those things of which we have not learned accurately from the divine Scriptures. For how is it possible for those to do this who overturn the doctrines of others? But to those who wish to learn the accurate word from us, we shall say, being persuaded by the holy Apostle, that we know it is proper for us to see the hidden mysteries in this way, just as he himself said: 'For now we see in a mirror, in a riddle; then face to face. Now we know in part; then I shall know just as I also am known' (1 Cor 13:12).

So do not inquire of me about things of which I have not learned clearly from the divine Scripture. Therefore, indeed, I will not be able to speak clearly even about that divine flesh which partook of the divine Word. But now I believe the divine Scriptures: that there is one God, and this [one God's] Word proceeded from the Father, so that 'all things might be through Him' (John 1:10), and after the time of judgment, and the correction of all things, and the destruction of every opposing energy, 'then He himself shall submit to Him who subjected all things to Him' (1 Cor 15:28), 'to God and Father,' so that the Word might be in God, just as He also was before the world existed. For nothing existed before except God alone, and since all things were to come into being through the Word, the Word proceeded with an active energy, the Word being of the Father.

This is he about whom Paul said, 'the predestined Son of God' (Rom 8:29). For this reason the most holy prophet Solomon said, 'to receive turns of speech,' and again, 'utterances of the wise and riddles.' Therefore, it seems to me that this most wise prophet has spoken the first words of prophecy proverbially. For nothing is incongruous, I think, in the present little of the...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Proverb of Letters and the Goat
english: One might recall you through proverbs. But either it is dead or it teaches letters. Someone might take this proverb to refer to the appearance of the letter, saying that those teaching according to the letters are doing so; for another also said among them, 'You were teaching letters, but I was plundering.'

But those who wrote the commentaries said it was not so; rather, because Sicilians, having won the war against the Athenians, they say, were saving only those carrying the educational staff, leading their teachers to the children while plundering all the others, they said that some of them, having fled and returned, were asked by the Athenians about certain things differing from them, and they said, 'But either it is dead or it teaches letters.'

And what about 'The goat [has] the knife'? Someone might think [it was said] so that he might first say the things said about it, in order to somehow divert the proverb because of the goat being sacrificed to the knife. But the ancients did not say this; for the said thing would not have been a proverb, if it had been like this (for this would have been easy to perceive from the appearances), but they say it was said regarding those bringing evils upon themselves. For they say that Medea, having killed the children in Corinth, hid the knife on the spot; and the Corinthians, while sacrificing a black goat given to them by lot, were at a loss for knives, and the goat, scratching with its foot, found the knife of Medea and was sacrificed by it.

And what does 'The sow [is an] oak' mean? Someone says: for it is not possible to recognize the proverb from what is at hand. The ancients, as they said, while eating acorns before the agriculture of wheat, because they thought this fruit would be found later, paying attention to it and rejoicing in the change, said 'The sow is an oak'; and they said this was the proverb.

Again, there is another proverb mentioned by many of the wise among them in many and diverse books; what some have written about it, those who set themselves to interpret proverbs, it is necessary in the present to mention [...], but in order that we may expose Asterius, and that he, being a man knowing the sciences of the external [sources] exactly, the excellence of the proverb, but in the present having feigned ignorance, might seem to be skillfully constructing his own will through the use of the proverbial phrase.

And there is 'The Art of Glaucus'. This, the external wise men, having remembered the proverb, explained it diversely. For one of them said that a certain Glaucus, having become a master of a certain art, the being very wonderful of many, perished at once in the sea, with no one at all proclaiming it. Another, testifying to the experience in music at the highest, says that four bronze discs constructed by him were for the purpose of making the harmony of the sounds somewhat pleasant; from this the proverb is said to be. Another indeed says that a wonderful crater and an under-crater of Alyattic votive offerings are standing, the work of Glaucus of Chios. Another, to place Glaucus himself as a bronze tripod in Delphi, having thus created it, to make the thick-sounding legs upon which he stands, and the upper surrounding part and the crown upon the basin and the rods arranged through the middle, to speak with the voice of a lyre. And again another, from a certain Glaucus having thought to have done more, says the proverb.

You see how the difficulty of the proverb is shown, through the fact that those wishing to explain this proverb do not even stand upon the same interpretation. Thus something difficult the matter of the proverb seems to be even among the external [ones]. Therefore also someone, having collected the proverbs said by many and diversely among the wise with them, has written six books about them, two of the metrical and four of the unmetered. And these proverbs the external ones named 'Proverbs' for no other reason, it seems to me, but because having encountered the Proverbs of the wisest Solomon and having known through them that there is nothing to learn clearly from what is said in them by what is at hand, and themselves having wished to emulate the prophetic [style], they wrote the letters in the same manner as he. Then, as being unable to devise any other name more important than that, they named these 'Proverbs'.

So surely this is 'The Lord has created me for the beginning of his ways toward his works' (Proverbs 8:22). (He says) that the Word of God prepared the human flesh to become immortal through the resurrection and just as a crown of victory...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: Letter to Julius regarding false accusations
english: [He is] having sat down at the right hand of the Father. He says that he has made this by composing one single treatise for the purpose of knowing God. Greetings to the most blessed co-celebrant Julius from Marcellus in Christ.

Because certain ones, having been previously convicted of not believing correctly—whom I refuted at the Council of Nicaea—dared to write to your piety against me, striving to transfer their own guilt onto me as if I were not thinking correctly even ecclesiastically, I deemed it necessary to respond by reminding you, so that you might send those who wrote against me to be refuted by me on both sides, since also what they have written against me turns out to be false, and that even now they persist in their former plan and have dared to be terrible both against the churches of God and against us who preside over them.

Since, therefore, they were not willing to respond, having sent your presbyters to them, and since I have completed this in Rome for a total of three years and one month, I deemed it necessary, as I am about to depart from here, to write my faith to you with all truth, having written it with my own hand, to hand it over to you, which I learned both from the divine Scriptures and from the bad things said by them, and to remind you, so that you may know those who wish to use the truth to hide it for the purpose of deceiving those who listen to the words.
For they say that the word of the Pantokrator God is not one's own and true...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Son vs. a different Logos
english: [They say that it is not] the Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, [but] a different word of him and a different wisdom and power. Because he was named word and wisdom and power by him, they claim that a different substance standing apart from the Father exists, because they think in this way.

Furthermore, they also claim that the Father pre-existed the Son, through which they venture to argue, and that he is not truly the Son of God; but even if they say 'of God', they say it in the same way as [they say] 'all things'. Moreover, they even dare to say that there was once a time when he was not, and that he is a creature and a work, distinguishing him from the Father.

Therefore, I believe those saying these things to be strangers to the Catholic Church. But I believe, following the divine Scriptures, that there is one God and his only-begotten Son, the Word, who is always co-existing with the Father and has never possessed a beginning of being, truly existing from God, not having been created, not having been made, but always being, always reigning with 'God and Father', whose 'kingdom', according to the testimony of the apostle, 'will have no end' (Rev 11:15).
This is the Son, this is the power, this is the wisdom. This is the same and true Word of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, the undivided power of [...]
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Logos and the Creed
english: Of God, through whom all things that came into being came to be, just as the Gospel testifies saying, 'In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. All things through him came to be, and without him nothing came into being' (John 1:1-3). This is the Word about whom also Luke the evangelist testifies saying, 'just as we were handed down by those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word' (Luke 1:2). Concerning this also David said, 'My heart has searched out a good word' (Psalm 40:8). So also our Lord Jesus Christ teaches us through the Gospel saying, 'I went out from the Father and I have come' (John 16:28).
This one, having descended 'in the last days' (Matthew 28:20) for our salvation and having been born of the virgin Mary, took upon himself the man.

I believe therefore in God the almighty; and in Christ Jesus his son, the only-begotten, our Lord, born of the Holy Spirit and Mary the virgin, having been crucified under Pontius Pilate and having been buried and on the third day having risen from the dead, having ascended into the heavens and sitting at the right hand of the Father, from where he comes to judge the living and the dead; and in the Holy Spirit, the holy church, the forgiveness of sins, the flesh...
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.

title: The Indivisibility of the Godhead
english: [the] resurrection, eternal life. We have learned from the divine writings that the divinity of the Father and of the Son is to be indivisible.

For if anyone separates the Son, that is, the Word of the Pantokrator God, it is necessary for him either to think them to be two gods (which has been considered alien to the divine teaching) or to confess that the Word is not God (which also appears to be alien to the right faith, the Evangelist saying, "and the Word was God" [John 1:1]). But I have learned precisely that the Son of the Father is indivisible and inseparable in power.

For the Savior himself, the Lord our Jesus Christ, says, "the Father is in me, and I in the Father" [John 14:10], and "I and the Father are one" [John 10:30], and "he who has seen me has seen the Father" [John 14:9]. This faith I have received from the divine writings and have been taught by the ancestors according to God, and in the church of God I preach and to you now I have written, possessing the counterpart of this with myself.

And I permit the antitype of this to be inscribed in the letter to the bishops, so that some of those not knowing precisely might be deceived by paying attention to those writing under them. Farewell.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
